questions.statement: Roleplay: You meet your teacher in the corridor. Which greeting opens the dialogue politely?
questions.context: Lucia is rehearsing polite greetings for a roleplay exam.

options.text: Good morning, Mrs Ruiz, how are you?
options.feedback: Correct! Good morning, Mrs Ruiz, how are you is polite because the greeting plus title and question shows respect to a teacher.

options.text: Yo, give me your notes right now.
options.feedback: The phrase Yo, give me your notes is wrong because slang plus a blunt demand sounds rude and unsuitable for greeting a teacher.

options.text: Whatever, I am busy at the moment.
options.feedback: The phrase Whatever, I am busy now is wrong because it dismisses the listener and fails to open any friendly conversation.

options.text: Shut up and listen to me now.
options.feedback: The phrase Shut up and listen to me is wrong because it is aggressive and cannot function as a polite greeting in any roleplay.

questions.explanation: Polite greetings open conversations with friendly phrases. Good morning and How are you suit formal and semi formal roleplays with teachers.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Roleplay: You need help in a shop. Which request sounds polite and appropriate?
questions.context: Marco is learning how to make polite requests in dialogues.

options.text: Could you help me with this bag, please?
options.feedback: Correct! Could you help me with this bag please is polite because the modal plus please turns a need into a respectful request.

options.text: Give me that bag right now.
options.feedback: The order Give me that bag now is wrong because the imperative plus now sounds like a command and lacks any polite softening.

options.text: What is your problem today?
options.feedback: The question What is your problem today is wrong because it challenges the listener instead of requesting help with the bag.

options.text: I do not need anyone here.
options.feedback: The statement I do not need anyone here is wrong because it rejects help and performs the opposite function of a polite request.

questions.explanation: Polite requests use Could you, Would you mind or Please with soft intonation. Direct orders sound rude in service roleplays and shops.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Friends plan a holiday. Which line makes a friendly suggestion?
questions.context: Sara is practising suggestions for a group holiday roleplay.

options.text: Shall we visit the old castle tomorrow?
options.feedback: Correct! Shall we visit the old castle tomorrow is a suggestion because Shall we invites friends to agree on a joint holiday plan.

options.text: Clean your room at once, please.
options.feedback: The order Clean your room at once is wrong because it commands action at home and makes no holiday proposal to the group.

options.text: What time is breakfast today?
options.feedback: The question What time is breakfast today is wrong because it only asks for information and proposes no shared activity.

options.text: I hate castles and old museums.
options.feedback: The statement I hate castles and museums is wrong because it expresses dislike and blocks rather than suggesting a group plan.

questions.explanation: Suggestions in speaking use Shall we, How about or Why not with a proposal. They invite agreement rather than giving orders to friends.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A: City buses are very useful. B: ??? Which reply agrees politely?
questions.context: Pablo is studying how to agree politely in conversations.

options.text: I agree, buses save money and cut traffic.
options.feedback: Correct! I agree, buses save money and cut traffic is polite agreement because it confirms the idea and adds a clear supporting reason.

options.text: No way, that idea is completely stupid.
options.feedback: The phrase No way, that is stupid is wrong because it rudely rejects the partner and breaks polite agreement in the dialogue.

options.text: Sorry, I was not listening at all.
options.feedback: The phrase I was not listening at all is wrong because it admits inattention and fails to confirm or support the bus idea.

options.text: Buses are boring, so stop talking.
options.feedback: The phrase Buses are boring, stop talking is wrong because it dismisses the topic and closes rather than agreeing with the partner.

questions.explanation: Agreeing phrases include I agree, Exactly and Good point. They confirm the partner idea before adding reasons, which keeps turn taking smooth.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A: Morning study is best. Which reply disagrees politely and keeps the dialogue open?
questions.context: Elena is learning to disagree without sounding rude.

options.text: I see your point, but night study suits me better.
options.feedback: Correct! I see your point, but night study suits me better is polite because the softener respects the partner before presenting a contrast.

options.text: You are totally wrong, you idiot.
options.feedback: The phrase You are totally wrong, idiot is wrong because insults and absolute rejection destroy polite disagreement in any dialogue.

options.text: Silence now, I know everything here.
options.feedback: The phrase Silence, I know everything here is wrong because it orders silence and claims superiority instead of softening opposition.

options.text: Whatever, nobody cares about exams.
options.feedback: The phrase Whatever, nobody cares about exams is wrong because dismissal avoids reasons and fails to disagree constructively.

questions.explanation: Polite disagreement softens opposition with I see your point but or I am not sure. It respects the partner before giving a different view.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Phone roleplay: You did not hear the address. What do you say to clarify?
questions.context: Diego is rehearsing how to ask for clarification on the phone.

options.text: Sorry, could you repeat the address slowly?
options.feedback: Correct! Sorry, could you repeat the address slowly is clarification because it names the problem and politely asks the speaker to say it again.

options.text: Fine, I got everything perfectly, bye.
options.feedback: The phrase Fine, I got everything perfectly is wrong because claiming full understanding blocks the clarification the situation clearly needs.

options.text: Stop talking now, I am very busy.
options.feedback: The phrase Stop talking, I am very busy is wrong because it ends the call rudely instead of requesting a slower repetition.

options.text: I know Madrid far better than you.
options.feedback: The phrase I know Madrid better than you is wrong because boasting about the city never asks for repetition of the unclear address.

questions.explanation: Clarification requests use Sorry, Could you repeat or What do you mean. They signal misunderstanding and invite the speaker to explain again.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Roleplay at the clinic. The doctor asks what is wrong. Which patient opening works best?
questions.context: Carmen is practising turn taking in a doctor roleplay.

options.text: I have had a sore throat for three days.
options.feedback: Correct! I have had a sore throat for three days is effective because it gives the symptom plus duration that the doctor needs for diagnosis.

options.text: Hello doctor, nice weather we have today.
options.feedback: The greeting Hello, nice weather today is wrong because weather chat delays symptoms and wastes the short medical appointment time.

options.text: Give me strong medicine immediately now.
options.feedback: The demand Give me medicine immediately now is wrong because requesting drugs before describing symptoms breaks the normal doctor sequence.

options.text: I really love hospitals and injections.
options.feedback: The joke I love hospitals and injections is wrong because humour about liking hospitals gives no useful symptom information at all.

questions.explanation: Patients describe symptoms clearly with I have a pain and how long. Doctors then ask follow up questions, so clear symptom reports open well.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Shop roleplay is over. Which line closes the conversation politely?
questions.context: Andres is learning how to close a dialogue politely.

options.text: Thanks for your help, see you soon.
options.feedback: Correct! Thanks for your help, see you soon is polite closing because thanks plus a future wish ends the shop exchange warmly and completely.

options.text: Go away now, I am done with you.
options.feedback: The phrase Go away, I am done now is wrong because ordering the assistant away after help sounds rude and abrupt.

options.text: You talk too much today, stop it.
options.feedback: The phrase You talk too much today is wrong because criticising the assistant cannot close a helpful exchange politely.

options.text: Wait here, I may return later.
options.feedback: The phrase Wait here, I may return is wrong because it leaves the ending open and fails to thank for the help received.

questions.explanation: Closings summarise and thank with Thanks for your help and See you soon. Abrupt goodbyes sound rude after a helpful service exchange.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Line: What time does the train to Sevilla leave? What is the function of this line?
questions.context: Lucia is identifying the function of short dialogue lines.

options.text: Asking for information about times.
options.feedback: Correct! Asking for information is right because What time does it leave requests a timetable fact rather than apologising or offering.

options.text: Apologising for a serious mistake.
options.feedback: The label apologising is wrong because no sorry or excuse appears and no fault is admitted in the station question.

options.text: Offering help with heavy bags.
options.feedback: The label offering help is wrong because the speaker requests facts instead of proposing assistance to the other person.

options.text: Complaining about a terrible service.
options.feedback: The label complaining is wrong because no dissatisfaction or criticism is expressed in the neutral timetable question.

questions.explanation: Identifying function means naming what the line does. Asking What time does it leave checks information, so its function is asking for details.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Roleplay in a restaurant. Which line orders food politely?
questions.context: Marco is memorising useful phrases for restaurant roleplays.

options.text: I would like a salad and some water.
options.feedback: Correct! I would like a salad and some water is polite ordering because would like softens the order into a courteous restaurant request.

options.text: Bring me food fast, I am hungry.
options.feedback: The order Bring food fast, I am hungry is wrong because the command plus hurry sounds rude to waiters in a restaurant.

options.text: This place smells badly today.
options.feedback: The complaint This place smells badly today is wrong because criticising the room cannot order salad or water politely.

options.text: Where is the toilet in this place?
options.feedback: The question Where is the toilet Paper is wrong because asking for facilities never orders the salad and water the roleplay needs.

questions.explanation: Ordering food politely uses I would like and Could we have. Pointing and shouting bypass polite service language expected in restaurants.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A: Where do you train for basketball? B: ??? Choose the coherent next line.
questions.context: Sara is choosing the natural next line in a dialogue.

options.text: At the sports centre, near the park.
options.feedback: Correct! At the sports centre near the park answers where because it gives the training place that the where question directly requests.

options.text: At midnight, together with the owls.
options.feedback: The reply At midnight with owls is wrong because a night time plus animals cannot answer a where question about training location.

options.text: Because I really like blue shirts.
options.feedback: The reply Because I like blue shirts is wrong because a reason about shirts answers why rather than where training happens.

options.text: I do not remember anything today.
options.feedback: The reply I do not remember anything today is wrong because forgetting everything avoids answering and breaks dialogue coherence.

questions.explanation: Next lines must match the question type. Where questions need places, so At the sports centre directly answers the training location question.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Friends choose a film. Which line is rude and breaks roleplay rules?
questions.context: Pablo is spotting rude lines that break roleplay rules.

options.text: Shut up, your idea is rubbish.
options.feedback: Correct! Shut up, your idea is rubbish is the rude line because the insult plus order breaks polite turn taking and respect rules.

options.text: How about watching a comedy film?
options.feedback: The polite suggestion How about a comedy film is not rude because it proposes an option softly and respects partner choice.

options.text: Good idea, I really love comedies.
options.feedback: The polite agreement Good idea, I love comedies is not rude because it confirms warmly and supports the partner proposal.

options.text: What time does the film start?
options.feedback: The clarification What time starts the film is not rude because it requests neutral information needed to plan the evening.

questions.explanation: Roleplays test register and politeness. Interrupting with orders or insults fails, while softeners and please keep the exchange appropriate.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A: You lost my book! Which apology works best in the roleplay?
questions.context: Elena is evaluating apologies in a lost book dialogue.

options.text: I am sorry, I lost it, I will buy a new one.
options.feedback: Correct! I am sorry, I will buy you a new one is best because sorry plus responsibility plus repair completes a full sincere apology.

options.text: I never borrowed any book from you.
options.feedback: The denial I never borrowed any book is wrong because refusing responsibility after losing the book blocks any sincere apology.

options.text: Books are boring anyway, just forget it.
options.feedback: The joke Books are boring, forget it is wrong because dismissing books as boring shows no regret and offers no repair for loss.

options.text: You should keep your books much safer.
options.feedback: The blame You should keep books safer is wrong because shifting fault to the owner reverses the apology and sounds unfair.

questions.explanation: Full apologies admit fault, show regret and offer repair. I am sorry, it was my fault plus I will buy a new one covers all three steps.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You must interrupt a friend urgently. Which interruption stays polite?
questions.context: Diego is analysing interruptions that stay polite.

options.text: Sorry to interrupt, but the bus leaves soon.
options.feedback: Correct! Sorry to interrupt, but the bus leaves soon is polite because sorry plus urgent reason justifies pausing without shouting.

options.text: Be quiet now, it is my turn to speak.
options.feedback: The shout Be quiet, it is my turn now is wrong because ordering silence and claiming the turn interrupts aggressively and rudely.

options.text: I have nothing to say about this today.
options.feedback: The whisper I have nothing to say today is wrong because withdrawing from talk performs no interruption function at all.

options.text: Your story is too long and rather dull.
options.feedback: The laugh Your story is too long and dull is wrong because mocking length insults the speaker instead of pausing politely.

questions.explanation: Polite interruptions use Sorry to interrupt but with a brief reason. They pause the partner respectfully instead of shouting over them.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A: Would you like to come to my party on Saturday? Choose the warm acceptance.
questions.context: Carmen is practising invitations and responses for parties.

options.text: I would love to come, what time is it?
options.feedback: Correct! I would love to come, what time is it shows acceptance because love plus a time question confirms attendance and plans arrival.

options.text: No, parties are stupid and boring.
options.feedback: The refusal No, parties are stupid and boring is wrong because rejection plus insult performs refusal rather than warm acceptance.

options.text: Where exactly do you live in town?
options.feedback: The question Where do you live exactly is wrong because asking the address alone never confirms whether you will attend the party.

options.text: Music at parties is always too loud.
options.feedback: The complaint Music is always too loud is wrong because criticising volume avoids accepting and sounds negative about the event.

questions.explanation: Accepting invitations shows joy plus confirmation. I would love to come, what time confirms attendance warmly and checks practical details.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Interview: Why are you a good worker? Which answer keeps a formal register?
questions.context: Andres is judging register in a job interview roleplay.

options.text: I arrived on time because I value punctuality.
options.feedback: Correct! I arrived on time because I value punctuality is formal because full grammar plus value shows respect suited to an interview.

options.text: I dunno, interviews and stuff are boring.
options.feedback: The slang I dunno, stuff is boring here is wrong because dunno and stuff mark informal slang unsuitable for a job interview.

options.text: Yeah cool, whatever you say, man.
options.feedback: The phrase Yeah, cool, whatever you say is wrong because yeah plus cool plus dismissal shows careless informal register.

options.text: Just hire me now, do not ask questions.
options.feedback: The order Just hire me, do not ask is wrong because demanding hiring without questions breaks respectful interview behaviour.

questions.explanation: Formal interviews need full sentences and respectful vocabulary. Slang like gonna or cool lowers register and harms the candidate image.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which line uses a question tag to invite agreement softly?
questions.context: Lucia is checking question tags that keep dialogues friendly.

options.text: The park is lovely, is not it?
options.feedback: Correct! The park is lovely, is not it invites agreement because the tag turns a statement into a soft friendly check for opinion.

options.text: Open the window right now.
options.feedback: The blunt order Open the window now is wrong because an imperative command gives no tag and invites no soft agreement.

options.text: Water boils at one hundred degrees.
options.feedback: The fact Water boils at one hundred degrees is wrong because a scientific fact states truth rather than inviting friendly agreement.

options.text: Your taste in parks is awful.
options.feedback: The insult Your taste in parks is awful is wrong because criticism attacks the partner instead of softly inviting shared opinion.

questions.explanation: Question tags like is not it and do you invite opinions softly. They turn statements into friendly checks rather than blunt declarations.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Call about homework notes. Which ending is clear and polite?
questions.context: Marco is evaluating how to end a phone call clearly.

options.text: I will send the notes tonight, thanks for calling.
options.feedback: Correct! I will send the notes tonight, thanks for calling is clear because the promise plus thanks confirms action and closes warmly.

options.text: Bye.
options.feedback: The abrupt Bye with no promise is wrong because hanging up without confirming the notes leaves the phone task unresolved.

options.text: Calls are annoying, please do not call again.
options.feedback: The complaint Calls are annoying, do not call is wrong because rejecting future calls ends rudely and never confirms the notes promise.

options.text: Maybe something will happen very soon.
options.feedback: The vague Maybe something will happen soon is wrong because vagueness confirms no action and leaves the caller without clear closure.

questions.explanation: Clear phone endings confirm action plus thanks. I will send the notes tonight, thanks for calling combines promise with polite closure.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Tourist: How do I get to the station? Which direction response works best?
questions.context: Sara is tackling a tricky roleplay on giving directions.

options.text: Go straight on and turn left at the bank.
options.feedback: Correct! Go straight and turn left at the bank is helpful because straight plus landmark gives an ordered visual route to the station.

options.text: It is over there somewhere, I think.
options.feedback: The vague It is over there somewhere is wrong because over there gives no steps or landmarks and leaves the tourist lost.

options.text: I never walk around this town myself.
options.feedback: The refusal I never walk around this town is wrong because avoiding personal habits gives no route to the requested station.

options.text: Why do you travel so much these days?
options.feedback: The question Why do you travel so much is wrong because asking motives answers no direction and ignores the where request.

questions.explanation: Good directions use sequence plus landmarks. Go straight, turn left at the bank is clear, while vague over there leaves listeners lost.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Ana wants football, Luis wants cinema. As mediator, what do you say to balance both?
questions.context: Pablo is facing the hardest task on mediating opinions.

options.text: You both want fun, so match in the morning, film later.
options.feedback: Correct! You both want fun, so match plus film works because it names shared goals and offers a compromise satisfying both partners.

options.text: Ana is right, forget football completely.
options.feedback: The siding Ana is right, forget football is wrong because taking one side abandons mediation and leaves one partner completely ignored.

options.text: Stop arguing now, I am leaving this place.
options.feedback: The avoidance Stop arguing, I am leaving now is wrong because leaving ends talk without balancing views or proposing any compromise.

options.text: Arguments are fun, so continue shouting loudly.
options.feedback: The joke Arguments are fun, continue shouting is wrong because encouraging shouting fuels conflict rather than mediating toward agreement.

questions.explanation: Mediating balances both views then proposes compromise. You both want fun, so a morning match plus an afternoon film satisfies each partner fairly.
questions.subject: ingles
